note: Leaves the left ventricle. The ascending aorta gives the coronary arteries; the arch gives the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian; it then descends through the thorax and abdomen and bifurcates at L4.
cl: the largest artery, leaving the left ventricle and bifurcating at L4

note: The first branch of the aortic arch, on the right only. It divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
cl: the first branch of the aortic arch, which divides into the right common carotid and right subclavian

note: The left arises from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk. Each divides at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into the internal and external carotid arteries.
cl: it divides at about C4 into the internal and external carotid arteries

note: Ascends in the neck without branching, enters the skull through the carotid canal and supplies the brain and the orbit.
cl: it has no branches in the neck and enters the skull through the carotid canal

note: Supplies the face, scalp, neck and jaw. Its terminal branches are the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
cl: its terminal branches are the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries

note: A branch of the subclavian artery. It ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and enters the skull through the foramen magnum; the two vertebral arteries join to form the basilar artery.
cl: it runs through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1 and joins its partner to form the basilar artery

n: Circle of Willis and cerebral arteries
note: An anastomosis at the base of the brain that links the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems. Drawn schematically here.
cl: an anastomotic ring at the base of the brain joining the carotid and vertebrobasilar supply

note: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk on the right and the aortic arch on the left. It becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib.
cl: it becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib

note: Runs from the lateral border of the first rib to the inferior border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery.
cl: it runs from the first rib to the inferior border of teres major

note: Runs down the medial side of the arm and divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa. It is the usual artery for blood pressure measurement.
cl: it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries in the cubital fossa

note: Arises from the brachial artery near the top of the arm and runs with the radial nerve in the spiral groove, supplying triceps. Its terminal branches join the arterial network around the elbow.
cl: the artery that runs with the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus

note: Runs down the lateral forearm. Its pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis. It forms the deep palmar arch.
cl: its pulse is felt at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis

note: Runs down the medial forearm, gives off the common interosseous artery, and mainly forms the superficial palmar arch.
cl: it mainly forms the superficial palmar arch

note: The superficial palmar arch is mainly the continuation of the ulnar artery. The deep palmar arch is formed by the radial artery, completed by the deep branch of the ulnar artery. Both give branches to the fingers.
cl: two arterial loops across the palm, fed by the ulnar and radial arteries

note: The aorta bifurcates at L4 into the two common iliac arteries. Each divides at the pelvic brim, in front of the sacroiliac joint, into the internal and external iliac arteries.
cl: it divides at the pelvic brim into the internal and external iliac arteries

note: Supplies the pelvic organs, the gluteal region and the perineum.
cl: it supplies the pelvic organs, the buttock and the perineum

note: Runs along the pelvic brim and becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament.
cl: it becomes the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament

note: Enters the thigh at the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, passes through the adductor hiatus and becomes the popliteal artery. The profunda femoris is its main branch.
cl: it enters the thigh at the mid-inguinal point and passes through the adductor hiatus

note: The main supply to the thigh muscles. It arises laterally from the femoral artery just below the inguinal ligament.
cl: it is the main supply to the thigh muscles and arises just below the inguinal ligament

note: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee. It divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries at the lower border of popliteus.
cl: it runs behind the knee and divides into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries

note: Passes through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment and continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery.
cl: it continues onto the dorsum of the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery

note: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery in front of the ankle. Its pulse is felt on the top of the foot, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.
cl: the artery whose pulse is felt on the top of the foot

note: Runs in the posterior compartment and passes behind the medial malleolus, where its pulse can be felt, before dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries.
cl: its pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus

note: Arises just below the knee, usually from the posterior tibial artery, and runs down beside the fibula. It supplies the lateral and posterior compartments of the leg.
cl: the artery that runs down beside the fibula and supplies the lateral compartment of the leg

note: Arises from the aorta at T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries. It supplies the foregut.
cl: it arises at T12 and divides into the left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries

note: The common hepatic artery comes from the coeliac trunk. It divides into the gastroduodenal artery and the proper hepatic artery, which supplies the liver and gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder.
cl: the branch of the coeliac trunk that heads for the liver

note: The smallest branch of the coeliac trunk. It gives oesophageal branches to the lower oesophagus, then runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach.
cl: the smallest branch of the coeliac trunk, running along the lesser curvature of the stomach

note: The largest branch of the coeliac trunk. It follows a winding course along the top of the pancreas to the hilum of the spleen, supplying the body and tail of the pancreas on the way.
cl: the largest branch of the coeliac trunk, winding along the top of the pancreas to the spleen

note: Arises from the aorta at L1 and supplies the midgut: from the duodenum to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon.
cl: it arises at L1 and supplies the midgut

note: Arises from the aorta at L3 and supplies the hindgut: the distal third of the transverse colon down to the upper rectum.
cl: it arises at L3 and supplies the hindgut

note: Arises from the aorta at about L1 to L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery. The right is longer because the aorta lies to the left of the midline.
cl: it arises just below the superior mesenteric artery and the right is the longer one

note: A branch of the external carotid artery. It crosses the lower border of the mandible at the front of masseter, where its pulse can be felt, and runs up the face beside the mouth and nose.
cl: the branch of the external carotid whose pulse is felt where it crosses the lower jaw

note: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery. It runs up in front of the ear to the scalp, where its pulse can be felt.
cl: the terminal branch of the external carotid whose pulse is felt in front of the ear

note: A terminal branch of the external carotid artery. It passes through the infratemporal fossa, and its first part gives off the middle meningeal artery.
cl: the terminal branch of the external carotid that crosses the infratemporal fossa

note: A branch of the maxillary artery. It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and runs beneath the pterion. Tearing it is the commonest cause of an extradural haematoma.
cl: the artery that enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and lies under the pterion

note: A branch of the subclavian artery. It runs down behind the costal cartilages, close to the edge of the sternum, giving anterior intercostal branches. It ends as the superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries. Surgeons use it as a graft in coronary bypass surgery.
cl: the subclavian branch that runs down behind the costal cartilages beside the sternum

note: Most arise from the thoracic aorta. In each space they run in the costal groove, between the vein above and the nerve below.
cl: the paired arteries that run in the costal groove between a vein and a nerve

note: A branch of the left coronary artery running in the anterior interventricular groove. It supplies the anterior left ventricle and most of the interventricular septum.
cl: it runs in the anterior interventricular groove

note: Arises from the left aortic sinus and soon divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries.
cl: the vessel arising from the left aortic sinus that divides almost at once

note: Arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove. It usually supplies the right atrium, right ventricle, and the SA and AV nodes.
cl: it arises from the right aortic sinus and runs in the right atrioventricular groove

note: A branch of the left coronary artery running in the left atrioventricular groove. It supplies the left atrium and the lateral and posterior left ventricle.
cl: it runs in the left atrioventricular groove

note: Formed behind the first right costal cartilage by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins. It drains the head, neck, upper limbs and thoracic wall into the right atrium.
cl: it is formed by the two brachiocephalic veins and drains into the right atrium

note: Formed by the union of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The left is longer and crosses in front of the branches of the aortic arch to join the right and form the superior vena cava.
cl: it is formed by the internal jugular and subclavian veins and the left one is longer

note: Drains the brain and neck. It runs in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries and joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
cl: it runs in the carotid sheath and drains the brain and neck

note: Forms behind the angle of the mandible and runs down over sternocleidomastoid to drain into the subclavian vein. It is easy to see in the neck.
cl: the superficial neck vein that crosses sternocleidomastoid on the way to the subclavian vein

note: Continues from the axillary vein at the outer border of the first rib. It passes in front of scalenus anterior and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
cl: the vein that crosses the first rib in front of scalenus anterior

note: The brachial veins (usually paired) accompany the brachial artery and unite to form the axillary vein, which becomes the subclavian vein at the lateral border of the first rib.
cl: the paired vessels that accompany the brachial artery

note: Runs up the outer (lateral) side of the arm and in the groove between deltoid and pectoralis major, before draining into the axillary vein.
cl: the superficial arm vein that runs up the lateral side and through the deltopectoral groove

note: Runs up the inner (medial) side of the forearm and arm. It pierces the deep fascia about half way up the arm and joins the deep veins to form the axillary vein.
cl: the superficial arm vein on the medial side that dives into the deep fascia

note: Links the cephalic and basilic veins across the front of the elbow. It is a common site for taking blood and inserting cannulas.
cl: the vein across the front of the elbow that is commonly used for taking blood

note: Drains the back wall of the thorax and abdomen. The azygos vein on the right arches over the root of the right lung to enter the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos veins on the left cross to join it. It also links the superior and inferior vena cavae, so it can carry blood round a blocked IVC.
cl: the venous system on the vertebral column that arches over the root of the right lung into the superior vena cava

note: Formed by the union of the common iliac veins at L5. It ascends on the right of the aorta, passes through the diaphragm at T8 and enters the right atrium.
cl: it is formed at L5 and passes through the diaphragm at T8

note: The external and internal iliac veins unite to form the common iliac vein. The two common iliac veins join at L5 to form the inferior vena cava.
cl: two of these join at L5 to form the inferior vena cava

note: The continuation of the femoral vein from behind the inguinal ligament. It joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.
cl: the vein that continues the femoral vein above the inguinal ligament

note: Drains the pelvic organs and the gluteal region. It joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.
cl: the vein draining the pelvic organs that joins the continuation of the femoral vein

note: Lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle (from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein). It is the continuation of the popliteal vein.
cl: it lies medial to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle

note: Begins on the dorsum of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus and runs up the medial side of the leg and thigh. It drains into the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction, a little below the inguinal ligament.
cl: the long superficial vein that passes in front of the medial malleolus

note: Starts on the outer side of the foot, passes behind the lateral malleolus and runs up the back of the calf beside the sural nerve. It drains into the popliteal vein.
cl: the superficial vein that passes behind the lateral malleolus and up the calf beside the sural nerve

note: Formed where the tibial veins join, behind the knee. In the popliteal fossa it lies between the tibial nerve (more superficial) and the popliteal artery (deeper). It continues as the femoral vein.
cl: the vein behind the knee that lies superficial to the artery there

note: The anterior and posterior tibial veins run with their arteries and join to form the popliteal vein.
cl: the deep veins of the calf that accompany the arteries of the leg

note: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It carries blood from the gut to the liver.
cl: it carries blood from the gut to the liver

note: Usually three veins (right, middle and left) that drain the liver straight into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
cl: the veins that carry blood from the liver directly into the inferior vena cava

note: Runs behind the pancreas and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.
cl: the vein that runs behind the pancreas and helps form the portal vein

note: Drains the small intestine and the right side of the large bowel. It joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.
cl: the vein draining the small intestine that joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein

note: Drains the hindgut: the distal transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon and the upper rectum. It usually ends by joining the splenic vein, though it can join the superior mesenteric vein instead.
cl: the vein of the hindgut that usually ends in the splenic vein

note: The left renal vein is longer than the right. It passes in front of the aorta, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, while the short right vein goes straight to the inferior vena cava.
cl: the vein that carries blood from the kidney, with the left one crossing in front of the aorta

note: Runs down the neck through the transverse foramina with the vertebral artery and drains into the brachiocephalic vein.
cl: the neck vein that travels through the transverse foramina with an artery

note: Blood-filled channels between the layers of the dura mater that drain the brain. They have no valves and end in the internal jugular veins.
cl: the valveless channels between layers of dura that drain the brain

note: Forms most of the back (base) of the heart and receives the four pulmonary veins. It empties through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
cl: the chamber that receives the pulmonary veins

note: Receives the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus. The fossa ovalis, the remnant of the foramen ovale, lies on its septal wall.
cl: the chamber that receives the venae cavae and has the fossa ovalis on its septum

note: Has the thickest wall, forms the apex of the heart and pumps blood into the aorta through the aortic valve.
cl: the thickest-walled chamber, forming the apex of the heart

note: Forms most of the front surface of the heart. It pumps blood to the lungs through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
cl: the chamber that forms most of the front of the heart and pumps blood to the lungs

note: Two atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) and two semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic).
cl: the four structures that keep blood moving one way through the cardiac chambers

note: Muscle projections inside the ventricles. Chordae tendineae tie them to the cusps of the atrioventricular valves, which stops the cusps prolapsing back into the atria.
cl: the muscle projections in the ventricles joined to valve cusps by chordae tendineae

note: The great, middle and small cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus on the back of the heart, which opens into the right atrium.
cl: the veins on the back of the heart that drain into the right atrium

note: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle. It divides under the aortic arch into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
cl: it carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle and divides into two

note: The right and left pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the lungs.
cl: it carries deoxygenated blood to a lung

note: Four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) carry oxygenated blood to the left atrium. They are the only veins that carry oxygenated blood.
cl: it carries oxygenated blood from a lung to the left atrium

note: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6) and ends at the carina, at about the level of the sternal angle (T4 to T5), where it divides into the right and left main bronchi. It is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage.
cl: a tube held open by C-shaped cartilage rings that divides at the carina

note: The trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi, which divide into lobar (secondary) bronchi (three on the right, two on the left) and then segmental bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled foreign bodies lodge there more often. Branching pattern drawn schematically.
cl: the right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left

note: Has two lobes (upper and lower) divided by the oblique fissure. It has a cardiac notch and the lingula on its upper lobe.
cl: the lung with two lobes, a cardiac notch and a lingula

note: Has three lobes (upper, middle and lower) divided by the oblique and horizontal fissures.
cl: the lung with three lobes and a horizontal fissure

note: A leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage behind the root of the tongue. It tips back to cover the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.
cl: the flap of elastic cartilage that covers the laryngeal inlet when swallowing

note: Taste and general sensation from the front two thirds come from the chorda tympani (VII) and the lingual nerve (V3). The back third is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). All the muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus (vagus).
cl: the muscular organ with a split sensory supply: lingual and chorda tympani in front, glossopharyngeal behind

note: The parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands. The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar, and the facial nerve divides within the parotid gland.
cl: the paired glands whose largest member is crossed by the facial nerve branches

note: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that runs from the pharynx (C6) behind the trachea and heart, passes through the diaphragm at T10 and joins the stomach at the cardia. The upper third is skeletal muscle, the lower third smooth muscle.
cl: a muscular tube that passes through the diaphragm at T10

note: Lies in the left upper quadrant. Its parts are the cardia, fundus, body and pylorus, with the lesser and greater curvatures. Rugae line the mucosa. The pylorus lies near the transpyloric plane (L1).
cl: a J-shaped organ with a fundus, body and pylorus, and greater and lesser curvatures

note: The first and shortest part of the small intestine (about 25 cm). It forms a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas and receives bile and pancreatic juice at the major duodenal papilla.
cl: a C-shaped loop around the head of the pancreas

note: Together about 3 to 5 m long in life. The jejunum (upper left) has prominent circular folds and the ileum (lower right) has Peyer patches; both are suspended on the mesentery and absorb most nutrients. Coiling is schematic.
cl: the coiled part of the small intestine suspended on the mesentery

note: A narrow blind-ended tube arising from the caecum, where the taeniae coli meet. Its tip is most often found behind the caecum (retrocaecal).
cl: the narrow blind-ended tube arising from the caecum where the taeniae coli meet

note: Caecum, ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon, then rectum and anal canal. The colon has taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae; the ascending and descending parts are retroperitoneal.
cl: it has taeniae coli, haustra and appendices epiploicae

note: Intraperitoneal, hanging from the transverse mesocolon. The proximal two thirds come from the midgut (superior mesenteric artery) and the distal third from the hindgut (inferior mesenteric artery).
cl: the part of the large bowel that hangs from its own mesocolon at the midgut-hindgut junction

note: Retroperitoneal, running down the left flank from the splenic flexure to the sigmoid colon. Supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery.
cl: the retroperitoneal part of the large bowel on the left flank

note: An S-shaped loop of large bowel hanging on the sigmoid mesocolon between the descending colon and the rectum. Diverticular disease and volvulus often affect it.
cl: the S-shaped loop of large bowel on a mesocolon between the descending part and the rectum

note: The largest solid organ, in the right hypochondrium under the diaphragm. It has right and left lobes, with the caudate and quadrate lobes on its visceral surface. It receives blood from the hepatic artery and portal vein.
cl: the largest solid organ, in the right hypochondrium

note: Stores and concentrates bile on the underside of the liver. Its fundus projects at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage. The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct.
cl: it stores bile and its fundus lies at the tip of the right ninth costal cartilage

note: Lies retroperitoneally across L1 to L2 behind the stomach. It has a head (in the duodenal C-loop), neck, body and tail that reaches the splenic hilum. It has exocrine (digestive enzyme) and endocrine (islets of Langerhans) functions.
cl: a retroperitoneal gland with head, neck, body and tail, with exocrine and endocrine parts

note: Lies in the left upper quadrant behind the stomach, under ribs 9 to 11. It is the largest lymphoid organ and filters blood. A palpable spleen is enlarged.
cl: it lies under ribs 9 to 11 and filters blood

note: Retroperitoneal, either side of the vertebral column from about T12 to L3, with the right usually slightly lower because of the liver. Each has a cortex, medulla and renal pelvis, and the hilum transmits the renal vessels and ureter.
cl: a retroperitoneal organ with a cortex, medulla and renal pelvis

note: The funnel-shaped upper end of the ureter inside the kidney, formed where the major calyces join. It becomes the ureter at the pelviureteric junction.
cl: the funnel-shaped upper end of the ureter inside the kidney

note: About 25 cm long. It runs down on psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder. Three constrictions: pelvicureteric junction, pelvic brim, and vesicoureteric junction.
cl: it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery

note: Lies behind the pubic symphysis when empty and rises into the abdomen as it fills. The trigone, a smooth triangle on the posterior wall, is bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.
cl: it lies behind the pubic symphysis and has a smooth triangular trigone

note: Carries urine from the bladder to the outside. The male urethra is long (about 20 cm) and passes through the prostate and penis, while the female urethra is short (about 4 cm).
cl: the tube that carries urine out of the bladder

note: Two lobes joined by an isthmus lying over the upper tracheal rings, at about C5 to T1. It makes thyroxine (T4), tri-iodothyronine (T3) and calcitonin.
cl: a gland of two lobes and an isthmus in front of the trachea

note: Usually four small glands on the back of the thyroid. They make parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium.
cl: the small glands on the back of the thyroid that raise blood calcium

note: Sits on the upper pole of each kidney. The cortex makes corticosteroids (aldosterone, cortisol) and androgens; the medulla makes adrenaline and noradrenaline.
cl: it sits on the upper pole of the kidney, with a cortex and a medulla

note: Sits in the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, hanging from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum. The optic chiasm lies just above it, so a large pituitary tumour can cause visual field loss.
cl: the gland in the sella turcica below the optic chiasm

note: A small gland in the midline at the back of the third ventricle. It makes melatonin.
cl: the small midline gland behind the third ventricle that makes melatonin

note: Lies in the anterior superior mediastinum behind the sternum. T cells mature here. It is large in children and is gradually replaced by fat with age.
cl: the lymphoid organ behind the sternum where T cells mature

note: Sits in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. It is part of the ring of lymphoid tissue round the throat (Waldeyer’s ring).
cl: the lymphoid tissue between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches

note: Carries smell from the roof of the nose through the holes of the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb. A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell.
cl: the nerve that passes through the cribriform plate

note: Carries vision from the retina through the optic canal to the optic chiasm, where fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross.
cl: the nerve for vision that runs back to the chiasm

note: Enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. It supplies levator palpebrae superioris and all the eye muscles except superior oblique and lateral rectus. It also carries parasympathetic fibres to the pupil and ciliary muscle.
cl: the nerve supplying most eye muscles, the eyelid lifter and the constrictor of the pupil

note: The only cranial nerve to leave the back of the brainstem. It crosses within the midbrain and supplies superior oblique on the opposite side from its nucleus.
cl: the only cranial nerve to leave the back of the brainstem

note: The main sensory nerve of the face. Its three divisions leave the skull through the superior orbital fissure (V1), foramen rotundum (V2) and foramen ovale (V3). V3 also supplies the muscles of mastication.
cl: the main sensory nerve of the face, with three divisions leaving through three different foramina

note: Passes through the superior orbital fissure to supply lateral rectus. Its long course makes it vulnerable, and damage leaves the eye unable to look outwards.
cl: the nerve to lateral rectus

note: Leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen and divides in the parotid gland into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches. It supplies the muscles of facial expression and carries taste from the front of the tongue.
cl: the nerve that divides inside the parotid gland to supply the muscles of expression

note: Carries hearing (cochlear part) and balance (vestibular part) through the internal acoustic meatus.
cl: the nerve for hearing and balance

note: Leaves through the jugular foramen. It carries taste and general sensation from the back third of the tongue, supplies stylopharyngeus and gives parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland.
cl: the nerve for the back third of the tongue that supplies stylopharyngeus

note: Leaves through the jugular foramen and runs down the neck in the carotid sheath. It gives parasympathetic supply to the thorax and to the gut as far as roughly the left colic flexure. The recurrent laryngeal nerves loop under the right subclavian artery and the aortic arch.
cl: the long nerve running down the carotid sheath with a parasympathetic supply to the thorax and gut

note: Its spinal root rises through the foramen magnum and the nerve leaves through the jugular foramen. It supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, and runs in the posterior triangle of the neck, where it is at risk in surgery.
cl: the nerve for sternocleidomastoid and trapezius that crosses the posterior triangle

note: Leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal and supplies the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus. If it is damaged, the tongue deviates towards the weak side.
cl: the nerve through the canal in the occipital bone to the tongue muscles

note: V1 (ophthalmic) supplies the forehead and upper eyelid. V2 (maxillary) supplies the cheek and upper lip. V3 (mandibular) supplies the lower lip and chin, and the general sensation of the front of the tongue.
cl: the three sensory divisions of the face

note: Formed from the anterior rami of C5 to T1. It passes between scalenus anterior and scalenus medius, runs behind the clavicle and enters the axilla. The order is roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
cl: the network from C5 to T1 that passes between the scalenes and enters the axilla

note: C5 to C7. A branch of the lateral cord that pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the muscles of the front of the arm: coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis. It carries on as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
cl: the nerve that pierces coracobrachialis and supplies the front of the arm

note: C5 and C6. A branch of the posterior cord that passes through the quadrangular space round the surgical neck of the humerus. It supplies deltoid and teres minor.
cl: the nerve that runs through the quadrangular space round the surgical neck of the humerus

note: C5 to T1. A branch of the posterior cord that winds round the humerus in the spiral groove, supplying triceps. In the forearm it supplies the extensors, dividing near the elbow into a superficial (sensory) branch and the posterior interosseous nerve.
cl: the nerve in the spiral groove that supplies triceps and the extensor muscles

note: C5 to T1. It runs down the arm beside the brachial artery, passes between the heads of pronator teres and goes through the carpal tunnel. It supplies most forearm flexors, the thenar muscles and the lateral two lumbricals.
cl: the nerve that passes through the carpal tunnel

note: C8 and T1. It passes behind the medial epicondyle and enters the hand through Guyon’s canal, in front of the flexor retinaculum. It supplies flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus and most of the small muscles of the hand.
cl: the nerve that passes behind the medial epicondyle and through Guyon’s canal

n: Long thoracic, thoracodorsal and scapular nerves
note: The long thoracic nerve runs down the outer surface of serratus anterior and supplies it. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, the dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids and the suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
cl: the nerves that supply serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi and the shoulder-blade muscles

note: The anterior rami of T1 to T11. Each runs in the costal groove below the vein and artery, supplying the intercostal muscles and the skin of the chest wall. The lower ones continue to supply the abdominal wall. T12 forms the subcostal nerve.
cl: the nerves running below the artery in each costal groove

note: L2 to L4. It passes under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery and outside the femoral sheath. It supplies the quadriceps, sartorius and pectineus, and its saphenous branch supplies skin on the inner leg.
cl: the nerve that lies lateral to the main thigh artery under the inguinal ligament

note: L2 to L4. It leaves the pelvis through the obturator canal and supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh and the skin of the inner thigh.
cl: the nerve that passes through the canal in the pelvic wall to the adductors

note: L2 and L3. A purely sensory nerve that passes under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine and supplies the skin of the outer thigh. Squeezing it there causes meralgia paraesthetica.
cl: the purely sensory nerve of the outer thigh that passes under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS

note: L4 to S3. The largest nerve in the body. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, usually below piriformis, and divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
cl: the largest nerve in the body, leaving the pelvis usually below piriformis

note: A branch of the sciatic nerve that runs through the popliteal fossa and down the back of the leg, passing behind the medial malleolus. It divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves and supplies the muscles of the back of the leg and sole of the foot.
cl: the nerve that runs down the back of the leg and behind the medial malleolus into the sole

note: A branch of the sciatic nerve that winds round the neck of the fibula, where it is easily injured. It divides into the superficial and deep fibular nerves.
cl: the nerve that winds round the neck of the fibula

note: A sensory nerve formed from branches of the tibial and common fibular nerves. It runs down the back of the calf beside the small saphenous vein and behind the lateral malleolus to supply the outer side of the foot.
cl: the sensory nerve that runs beside the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus

note: The superior gluteal nerve (above piriformis) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae. The inferior gluteal nerve (below piriformis) supplies gluteus maximus. The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) leaves through the greater sciatic foramen and returns through the lesser one to reach the perineum.
cl: the nerves leaving the greater sciatic foramen to the buttock and perineum

note: Branches of the lumbar plexus. The iliohypogastric and ilio-inguinal nerves (L1) supply the lower abdominal wall and groin, and the ilio-inguinal nerve runs through the inguinal canal. The genitofemoral nerve (L1 and L2) supplies cremaster and skin of the groin. They can be injured in groin surgery.
cl: the lumbar nerves of the groin and lower abdominal wall

note: A chain of ganglia either side of the vertebral column, from the base of the skull to the coccyx. Preganglionic fibres enter from T1 to L2, and grey rami carry fibres back to the spinal nerves.
cl: the chain of ganglia beside the vertebral column

note: The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord (the conus medullaris, usually at about L1 to L2). They lie in the lumbar cistern, which is why a lumbar puncture below the cord is safe.
cl: the bundle of nerve roots that lies below the end of the spinal cord

note: Runs down the vertebral canal from the foramen magnum and ends at the conus medullaris at about L1 to L2 in adults; below that the lumbar and sacral nerve roots form the cauda equina.
cl: it ends at the conus medullaris at L1 to L2, below which is the cauda equina

note: Planning, personality and voluntary movement. The primary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus, and Broca’s area (speech production) is usually on the left.
cl: the lobe with the primary motor cortex

note: Receives touch and body position sensation in the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) and helps with spatial awareness.
cl: the lobe with the primary somatosensory cortex

note: Hearing, memory and language understanding. The primary auditory cortex is here, and Wernicke’s area is on the dominant (usually left) side.
cl: the lobe with the primary auditory cortex

note: Vision. It contains the primary visual cortex at the back of the brain.
cl: the lobe at the back that holds the primary visual cortex

note: Hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by parts of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. It is involved in taste and awareness of the body’s internal state.
cl: the lobe hidden in the lateral sulcus under the opercula

note: Sits above the corpus callosum on the inner surface of the hemisphere. It is part of the limbic system.
cl: the fold of cortex above the corpus callosum

note: Lies in the posterior cranial fossa below the tentorium cerebelli. It coordinates movement and balance, and each half acts on the same side of the body.
cl: the structure in the posterior cranial fossa that coordinates movement and balance

note: The midbrain, pons and medulla. Cranial nerves III to XII emerge from it, and it holds the centres that control breathing and heart rate.
cl: the midbrain, pons and medulla

note: A relay station that passes sensory information to the cerebral cortex. Smell is the exception.
cl: the relay station for sensory pathways to the cortex

note: Controls temperature, hunger, thirst and the body clock. It also directs the autonomic nervous system and the pituitary gland.
cl: the structure that controls temperature, hunger and thirst and directs the pituitary

note: Deep nuclei, including the caudate nucleus, putamen and globus pallidus, that help control movement. Parkinson’s disease involves loss of dopamine-making cells in the substantia nigra, which works closely with them.
cl: the deep nuclei including the caudate, putamen and globus pallidus

note: Lies in the medial temporal lobe and is vital for forming new memories.
cl: the medial temporal structure needed for forming new memories

note: Lies in the medial temporal lobe in front of the hippocampus. It processes emotion, especially fear.
cl: the almond-shaped nucleus in the medial temporal lobe that processes fear

note: The largest bundle of nerve fibres joining the two cerebral hemispheres.
cl: the largest fibre bundle joining the two hemispheres

note: Two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle. The choroid plexus makes CSF, which flows through the interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct and fourth ventricle, then out to the subarachnoid space.
cl: the CSF-filled cavities inside the cerebrum
